chunks.content: # CLO Shoe Making Process: Men's Shoe Tutorial and Techniques This document details the step-by-step procedures, technical methods, and practical tips for creating a pair of men's shoes using CLO software. It covers template loading, panel arrangement, sewing techniques, fabric application, simulation adjustments, and virtual model activation, with a focus on shoe base construction and precise alignment. --- ## Loading Templates and Initial Setup This section explains how to load the shoe template and corresponding virtual model into CLO, and prepare the template for shoe construction using positioning and duplication tools. - Load the shoe template into CLO. - Import the corresponding men's shoe virtual model. - Use an open horizontal position for the template. - Insert a split line at the position where the shoe board needs symmetry. - Use the shortcut Control + D to duplicate the board and floating line, ensuring symmetrical matching. - Move some boards to the 2D window, positioning them close to the virtual model for reference. - In the 3D window, reset the 2D board and place it in front of the model to start shoe making. --- ## Panel Selection and Positioning This section covers panel selection for the shoe excluding the bottom and side panels, saving materials, and arranging the shoe bottom with the positioning tool. - Select all panels except the bottom and side panels; save this selection as it is difficult to make shoe panels. - Open a physical surface view to distinguish the front and back of the panel, aiding in panel definition. - Use the positioning tool to arrange the bottom of the shoe in a positive, properly oriented state. - Since panels are small, select all and reduce their particle diameter to 5 for better manipulation. - Check the bottom's position from various angles, rotating as necessary. - Flip the bottom to the front position, ensuring its alignment with the foot bottom and ground contact. --- ## Board Duplication and Seamline Management This section details duplicating the outer layer of the shoe bottom board, removing unnecessary seamlines, and preparing for sewing. - Copy the outer layer of the board from the current position with the same direction and coordinates, avoiding the need for rearrangement. - Delete the sewing line on the bottom of the shoe. - Remove joints at the bottom to allow for future adjustments. - Confirm the effect by viewing the front of the shoe. --- ## Sewing Techniques and Board Assembly This section explains the sewing process for the shoe bottom and side panels, correcting sewing direction, and creating simulated thickness. - Sew the side of the shoe bottom, starting at the front of the foot and connecting around the back in a circular sewing line. - Define starting and ending points on the board for sewing. - Correct sewing direction if initially sewn incorrectly by reversing the sewing order.

chunks.content: --- ## Sewing Techniques and Board Assembly This section explains the sewing process for the shoe bottom and side panels, correcting sewing direction, and creating simulated thickness. - Sew the side of the shoe bottom, starting at the front of the foot and connecting around the back in a circular sewing line. - Define starting and ending points on the board for sewing. - Correct sewing direction if initially sewn incorrectly by reversing the sewing order. - Sew the top of the shoe to the top of the board, and the bottom of the shoe to the bottom of the board. - Sew the height of the side panels, establishing sewing relationships. - In the 3D window, select and move the side panels, then add them to the side to complete arrangement. - Open simulation to check the shape, confirming the shoe base consists of three boards: top layer, bottom layer, and side layer. - Adjust the folding angle of the sewing line from 180° to 90° to form a right-angle sewing angle, improving simulation quality. --- ## Fabric Application and Simulation Adjustments This section describes applying physical fabric to the shoe bottom edges, freezing layers for shape control, and simulating curvature to fit the foot. - Add fabric around the bottom side of the shoe using the physical fabric "Trim Hardware" provided in CLO. - Apply the fabric directly to the shoe base. - Freeze the upper and lower layers of the shoe base to control deformation during simulation. - Move one side of the shoe base to simulate adhesion to the foot. - Maintain a height gradient from front (lower) to back (higher) for realistic shoe base shape. - To create a flat shoe base near the foot with a curved bottom, freeze the top and bottom parts separately before simulation. - The board naturally simulates a flat bottom with a curved top to match foot curvature. --- ## Virtual Model Activation and Shoe Base Alignment This section covers activating the virtual model to create conflicts for adjustment, aligning the shoe base with the foot base, and refining shoe bottom height and curve points. - Activate the virtual model to enable conflict detection with shoe boards. - Adjust shoe base position so its bottom aligns closely with the foot base. - Convert and activate the shoe base after alignment. - Verify coincidence and alignment of the shoe base with the virtual foot by rotating the shoe forward. - Use curve point adjustment tools to fine-tune the bottom of the shoe. - Reduce excessive curve points on the shoe bottom sides for smoother shape control. - Freeze the shoe base after adjustment to prevent deformation. - Adjust shoe bottom height progressively, ensuring uniform modification over the entire bottom surface. --- ## Stock Removal and Shoelace Arrangement This section explains removing excess material (stock) from the shoe surface and arranging small boards like shoelaces using quick arrangement tools. - Remove stock from the entire shoe surface after finishing the base.

It emphasizes precision in panel arrangement, sewing direction correction, fabric application for realistic simulation, and the importance of freezing layers to maintain shoe shape integrity. The quick arrangement tool simplifies positioning smaller components such as shoelaces, streamlining the shoe design process.
